chunks.title: Two stock CAPM math
chunks.text: Let's pull out the cap M and take a look at this portfolio. Remember, for each individual stock, the expected return is beta times the return on the market plus alpha times the weight for that particular stock. And when we short, the weight is negative.

chunks.title: Two stock CAPM math
chunks.text: And we do this across all the stocks in our portfolio, and then that's our expected return for the portfolio. So I'm going to expand this sum. First, I'm going to start with the beta component. So we get weight A times beta A plus weight B times beta B times return on the market.

chunks.title: Two stock CAPM math
chunks.text: So recall the numbers from earlier. Our weights for A and B were each 0.5 and negative 0.5. We had a beta of 1 for A and a beta of 2 for B. For our alphas, we had plus 1% for stock A and negative 1% for stock B. We can plug all of these into our equation and work it out.

chunks.title: Two stock CAPM math
chunks.text: For our beta component, we end up with a beta for the portfolio of negative 0.5. Our alpha component for stock A ends up just being 0.5. And for stock B, negative 0.5 times negative 1, or 0.5. So bringing it all together, under these assumptions, using the cap M, our expected return for this allocation is negative 0.5 times the market return plus 1%.

chunks.title: Two stock CAPM math
chunks.text: Let's double check this by plugging in one of our earlier examples. Consider that example where the market went up 10%. So we've got minus 0.5 times 10% plus 1%. So in the case where the market goes up 10%, we expect a minus 4% return for our portfolio. So if you step back a little bit, remember that we arrived at this 1% using information.

chunks.title: Two stock CAPM math
chunks.text: So we have some information about these stocks that led us to believe one would go up 1% over the market, another would go down 1% over the market. On the other hand, we don't really have any knowledge about what's going to happen for the market overall. So we have no control over this component. Is there some way that we can remove this?

chunks.title: Two stock CAPM math
chunks.text: Can we make this part equal to 0? If we can do that, then we essentially remove market risk from our portfolio, and we preserve this 1% over here. Well, the way to do that is to focus on this part. Remember, this is beta for the portfolio.

chunks.title: Two stock CAPM math
chunks.text: Can we make beta for the portfolio equal to 0? Or in other words, can we find weights for A and B such that their sum turns out to be 0? What are these two weights so that the overall portfolio beta is 0?
